summary: This memo describes conventions used to encode Vietnamese characters in 7-bit US ASCII, called VIQR, and in an 8-bit form, called VISCII. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Vietnamese has many accents that old computers could not display. This paper describes two ways to write Vietnamese using the limited characters computers had.

questions: how do accents work in viqr
subtitle: Two ways to encode Vietnamese characters for older computers

tldr.problem: Vietnamese has 134 letter-and-diacritical combinations that don't fit the ASCII character set, making it hard to use on computers built for English.
tldr.mechanism: VISCII is an 8-bit encoding that assigns each Vietnamese letter with its diacritics a single code, while VIQR uses mnemonic ASCII characters (like a^ for a with circumflex) for 7-bit systems.
tldr.outcome: Vietnamese speakers could use email, documents, and software on the limited systems available in the 1990s, and these conventions remain in use today.

facts.label: VIQR diacritical marks
facts.value: 7 marks plus special d and D notations

today: RFC 1456 remains informational. Both VISCII and VIQR are obsoleted by Unicode for new applications, but the conventions continue to be used in legacy systems and in informal Vietnamese text exchange.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1456 describes VISCII and VIQR, two conventions for encoding Vietnamese text where computers and networks can only handle the basic 7-bit or 8-bit ASCII character set. These conventions let Vietnamese speakers send email, edit documents, and run programs without waiting for the world to upgrade to Unicode.

VISCII assigns a single 8-bit code to each Vietnamese letter with its accents (called diacritical marks). VIQR is simpler: it uses regular ASCII characters to stand in for the accents (like using ^ to show a circumflex). Both are mnemonic—easy to remember—so people can type Vietnamese using familiar keyboard patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Vietnamese letters have lots of funny marks on them. Instead of inventing new codes, these tricks let you write Vietnamese using characters that old computers understood.

sections.title: Why Vietnamese Needs Special Handling
sections.content:
Unlike French or Spanish, which add a handful of accented letters to the Latin alphabet, Vietnamese uses both a large number of accents (grave, acute, hook above, tilde, and dot below) and a large frequency of their use. Where French needs maybe 12 extra characters, Vietnamese needs 134 combinations. A keyboard designed for French can rely on a special "compose key" to build accented letters on demand, but Vietnamese text would require hundreds of compose sequences, making typing impractical.

The two solutions address different constraints. VISCII works in 8-bit systems where each letter gets its own code. VIQR works in 7-bit email systems, where every letter, accent, and punctuation must fit the basic ASCII set, making it human-readable even when the accents are lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Vietnamese has way more accents than French. You can't use special keys because you'd need too many of them. So people came up with two tricks that work on old computers.

sections.title: The Two Encodings
sections.content:
VISCII (VIetnamese Standard Code for Information Interchange) is an 8-bit code page, similar to ISO-8859/Latin-1. It reserves 256 slot numbers, assigns the 128 standard ASCII codes to English letters and symbols, and uses the remaining 128 codes for Vietnamese letters. Each Vietnamese character, with its accents pre-combined, gets a single code. VISCII retains the complete ASCII repertoire for compatibility, and even includes provisions for box-drawing characters used by the IBM PC.

VIQR (VIetnamese Quoted-Readable) is a text convention, not a code page. It represents Vietnamese by typing a base letter followed by an ASCII character that looks like the diacritical mark. The apostrophe ' represents acute (a'), the backtick ` is grave (a`), the caret ^ is circumflex (a^), the plus + is horn (o+), the parenthesis ( is breve (a(), the question mark ? is hook above (o?), the tilde ~ is tilde (a~), and the period . is dot below (a.). The RFC even includes a special notation for the bar through d and D (dd and DD).

Both systems have existing software support on Unix, MS-DOS, and Windows systems from the early 1990s onward, enabling Vietnamese users to take advantage of existing tools.
sections.plainLanguage: VISCII is like a secret code book where each Vietnamese letter has a number. VIQR is like writing the letter then writing a symbol that shows the accent—a' means a with acute. Both work, and both let people type and read Vietnamese easily.

sections.title: MIME Registration and Modern Use
sections.content:
For use with MIME (the Internet standard for email attachments and character sets), both VISCII and VIQR were registered as official character set names with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). This let email software label Vietnamese text correctly, so it would be decoded properly even if routed through multiple systems. A sender could mark a message as charset=VISCII or charset=VIQR, and any MIME-aware reader would know how to interpret it.

By registering these encodings, the RFC ensured that Vietnamese could be sent through the early Internet without loss of meaning, before Unicode became widespread. Today, Unicode (which includes all Vietnamese characters) has largely replaced these systems, but the conventions remain documented and in use in legacy systems and in informal Vietnamese online communities.
sections.plainLanguage: The email system was told about VISCII and VIQR so computers would know how to read Vietnamese text. Now we use better systems, but these rules still work for old emails and programs.
